examples_0408_B

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~{3}x^{4}+{4}x^{3}-{97}x^{2}-{244}x+{204}\]

One of the roots is \(-4+i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(-4+i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-4+i\) is a root, we also know \(-4-i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-4+i))(x-(-4-i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x+4-i)(x+4+i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-1i^2=1\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+8x+17)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+8x+17)~\equiv~{3}x^{4}+{4}x^{3}-{97}x^{2}-{244}x+{204}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{8}x+{17}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{3}x^{4}+{4}x^{3}-{97}x^{2}-{244}x+{204}}{x^{2}+{8}x+{17}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({3}x^{2}-{20}x+{12})(x^{2}+{8}x+{17})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-4+i\) and \(x=-4-i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{8}x+{17}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({3}x^{2}-{20}x+{12}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{3}x^{2}-{20}x+{12}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(-20)\pm\sqrt{(-20)^2-4(3)(12)}}{2(3)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{20\pm\sqrt{400-144}}{6}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{20\pm\sqrt{256}}{6}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{20\pm16}{6}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{20+16}{6} &&& x&=\frac{20-16}{6} \\\\ x&=\frac{36}{6} &&& x&=\frac{4}{6} \\\\ x&=6 &&& x&=\frac{2}{3} \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~(x-{6})({3}x-{2})(x-(-4+i))(x-(-4-i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~(x-{6})({3}x-{2})(x^{2}+{8}x+{17})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(6\) and \(\frac{2}{3}\).

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~{8}x^{4}+{2}x^{3}-{27}x^{2}-{58}x-{30}\]

One of the roots is \(-1+i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(-1+i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-1+i\) is a root, we also know \(-1-i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-1+i))(x-(-1-i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x+1-i)(x+1+i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-1i^2=1\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+2)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+2)~\equiv~{8}x^{4}+{2}x^{3}-{27}x^{2}-{58}x-{30}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{2}x+{2}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{8}x^{4}+{2}x^{3}-{27}x^{2}-{58}x-{30}}{x^{2}+{2}x+{2}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({8}x^{2}-{14}x-{15})(x^{2}+{2}x+{2})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-1+i\) and \(x=-1-i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{2}x+{2}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({8}x^{2}-{14}x-{15}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{8}x^{2}-{14}x-{15}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(-14)\pm\sqrt{(-14)^2-4(8)(-15)}}{2(8)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{14\pm\sqrt{196+480}}{16}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{14\pm\sqrt{676}}{16}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{14\pm26}{16}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{14+26}{16} &&& x&=\frac{14-26}{16} \\\\ x&=\frac{40}{16} &&& x&=\frac{-12}{16} \\\\ x&=\frac{5}{2} &&& x&=\frac{-3}{4} \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~({4}x+{3})({2}x-{5})(x-(-1+i))(x-(-1-i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~({4}x+{3})({2}x-{5})(x^{2}+{2}x+{2})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(\frac{-3}{4}\) and \(\frac{5}{2}\).

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~{12}x^{4}+{25}x^{3}-{9}x^{2}-{68}x-{70}\]

One of the roots is \(-1-i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(-1-i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-1-i\) is a root, we also know \(-1+i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-1-i))(x-(-1+i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x+1+i)(x+1-i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-1i^2=1\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+2)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+2)~\equiv~{12}x^{4}+{25}x^{3}-{9}x^{2}-{68}x-{70}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{2}x+{2}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{12}x^{4}+{25}x^{3}-{9}x^{2}-{68}x-{70}}{x^{2}+{2}x+{2}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({12}x^{2}+x-{35})(x^{2}+{2}x+{2})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-1-i\) and \(x=-1+i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{2}x+{2}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({12}x^{2}+x-{35}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{12}x^{2}+x-{35}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(1)\pm\sqrt{(1)^2-4(12)(-35)}}{2(12)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1+1680}}{24}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1681}}{24}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{-1\pm41}{24}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{-1+41}{24} &&& x&=\frac{-1-41}{24} \\\\ x&=\frac{40}{24} &&& x&=\frac{-42}{24} \\\\ x&=\frac{5}{3} &&& x&=\frac{-7}{4} \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~({3}x-{5})({4}x+{7})(x-(-1-i))(x-(-1+i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~({3}x-{5})({4}x+{7})(x^{2}+{2}x+{2})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(\frac{5}{3}\) and \(\frac{-7}{4}\).

\[f(x)~=~{45}x^{4}+{62}x^{3}+{38}x^{2}-{48}x+{8}\]

One of the roots is \(-1-i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(-1-i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-1-i\) is a root, we also know \(-1+i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-1-i))(x-(-1+i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+2)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+2x+2)~\equiv~{45}x^{4}+{62}x^{3}+{38}x^{2}-{48}x+{8}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{2}x+{2}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{{45}x^{4}+{62}x^{3}+{38}x^{2}-{48}x+{8}}{x^{2}+{2}x+{2}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~({45}x^{2}-{28}x+{4})(x^{2}+{2}x+{2})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-1-i\) and \(x=-1+i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{2}x+{2}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \({45}x^{2}-{28}x+{4}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[{45}x^{2}-{28}x+{4}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(-28)\pm\sqrt{(-28)^2-4(45)(4)}}{2(45)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{28\pm\sqrt{784-720}}{90}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{28\pm\sqrt{64}}{90}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{28\pm8}{90}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{28+8}{90} &&& x&=\frac{28-8}{90} \\\\ x&=\frac{36}{90} &&& x&=\frac{20}{90} \\\\ x&=\frac{2}{5} &&& x&=\frac{2}{9} \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~({9}x-{2})({5}x-{2})(x-(-1-i))(x-(-1+i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~({9}x-{2})({5}x-{2})(x^{2}+{2}x+{2})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(\frac{2}{9}\) and \(\frac{2}{5}\).

Let \(f\) represent a quartic (4th degree) polynomial with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~x^{4}-{5}x^{3}+x^{2}-{229}x+{232}\]

One of the roots is \(-2+5i\), where \(i=\sqrt{-1}\).

\[f(-2+5i)~=~0\]

This quartic polynomial has at least 1 rational root. Find all the rational roots.

We know that complex roots show up as complex-conjugate pairs. So, since \(-2+5i\) is a root, we also know \(-2-5i\) is another root. This accounts for two roots.

The fundamental theorem of algebra promises "every non-zero, single-variable, degree n polynomial with complex coefficients has, counted with multiplicity, exactly n complex roots."

So, we know there will be a total of 4 roots.

Thus, we should be able to express \(f(x)\) in a semi-factored form (with yet to be determined coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) and \(c\)).

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x-(-2+5i))(x-(-2-5i))\]

Distribute the negatives across the inner parentheses.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x+2-5i)(x+2+5i)\]

Now use a box to multiply the two complex factors.


Remember, \(i^2=-1\), so \(-25i^2=25\). Combine like terms.

\[f(x)~=~(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+4x+29)\]

Now... we know this semi-factored form and the standard form are equivalent expressions.

\[(ax^2+bx+c)(x^2+4x+29)~\equiv~x^{4}-{5}x^{3}+x^{2}-{229}x+{232}\]

So, we can divide both sides by \(x^{2}+{4}x+{29}\).

\[ax^2+bx+c~=~\frac{x^{4}-{5}x^{3}+x^{2}-{229}x+{232}}{x^{2}+{4}x+{29}}\]

Use the box method to divide.


So,

\[f(x)~=~(x^{2}-{9}x+{8})(x^{2}+{4}x+{29})\]

We have expressed the quartic polynomial as the product of two quadratic polynomials. Remember, our goal is to find solutions to \(f(x)=0\). We already know that \(x=-2+5i\) and \(x=-2-5i\) are solutions, and those two roots correspond to the factor \(x^{2}+{4}x+{29}\) equaling 0. By setting the other quadratic factor, \(x^{2}-{9}x+{8}\), equal to zero, we can find the other roots.

\[x^{2}-{9}x+{8}=0\]

Use the quadratic formula: if \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) then \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\).

\[x=\frac{-(-9)\pm\sqrt{(-9)^2-4(1)(8)}}{2(1)}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{9\pm\sqrt{81-32}}{2}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{9\pm\sqrt{49}}{2}\]

Simplify.

\[x=\frac{9\pm7}{2}\]

Split into two different fraction.

\[\begin{align} x&=\frac{9+7}{2} &&& x&=\frac{9-7}{2} \\\\ x&=\frac{16}{2} &&& x&=\frac{2}{2} \\\\ x&=8 &&& x&=1 \end{align}\]

Now we know all four roots. We could express \(f\) in fully factored form.

\[f(x)~=~(x-{8})(x-{1})(x-(-2+5i))(x-(-2-5i))\]

Or, if you are not into complex factors, you could also express \(f\) as factored as possible with integer coefficients.

\[f(x)~=~(x-{8})(x-{1})(x^{2}+{4}x+{29})\]

Anyway, the two rational roots are \(8\) and \(1\).
